To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the age-related muscle disease, sIBM, is characterized by inflammatory changes and amyloid deposition and may share pathogenetic mechanisms with the inflammatory and amyloid deposition changes in AD and atherosclerosis.

the age-related condition sIBM is associated with inflammatory changes that resemble atheromatous changes in vessels and senile plaquing in the brain and that these inflammatory changes are associated with the accumulation of Abeta peptides, which are derived from the amyloid precursor protein.

sIBM shares with normal aging and AD the accumulation of Abeta and other amyloidogenic proteins in the muscle and that sIBM can be induced by APP overexpression in mice, suggesting a role of APP in sIBM pathogenesis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the hypothesis that the pathogenic changes in sIBM may be the result of a complex interaction between the effects of aging and the presence of amyloid precursor protein and Abeta in the muscle.
the hypothesis that the aging changes in brain, muscle, vessels, and other organs are linked by common mechanisms.
the pathogenesis of sporadic inclusion-body (IBM) in muscle and the possibility of a common pathogenetic pathway with normal aging and AD.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
sIBM is a disease of the aging muscle that shares features of normal aging and of inflammatory diseases.

sIBM shares with aging and inflammatory conditions the following: (i) an age-related onset; (ii) an association with vascular changes; (iii) an increase in IL-1; (iv) the appearance of Abeta and other APP products, and (v) an association with atherosclerotic changes.
the pathogenesis of this disease remains obscure, and that the current state of the art is that it may be a form of amyloidosis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
aging and inflammation are important in the pathogenesis of the muscle, brain, and vessel changes in AD, sIBM, and vascular dementia.
the aging changes in muscle, vessels, and brain that occur in sIBM are not specific for this condition and that the changes in these tissues are interrelated.
the pathophysiological changes that are associated with sIBM, AD, and atheroma are all related to aging.
The main takeaway from our work is that
sIBM may be an inflammatory disease of muscle that is associated with the aging process and with the accumulation of Abeta peptides.
sIBM is a disease with a complex etiology, and that it shares some features of aging and AD.

the sIBM-like changes induced by APP transgenic expression are not specific to APP, because they also occur in a transgenic mouse model of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, in which APP is not expressed.
